sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: This chapter describes the information needed to design a soil nail wall, including subsurface investigation requirements, field and laboratory testing procedures, selection of design parameters, and evaluation of special conditions such as soil creep, corrosion potential, frost, and seismic loading. The subsurface investigation program must provide sufficient data to develop reliable design parameters, particularly soil shear strength and nail-ground bond strength.
key_points: Subsurface investigation requirements for soil nail wall design
Field and laboratory testing procedures
Selection of design parameters (shear strength, bond strength)
Evaluation of special conditions: creep, corrosion, frost, seismic
sections.applicability: All soil nail wall design projects requiring subsurface investigation.

sections.title: Subsurface Investigation
sections.body: The purpose of the subsurface investigation is to define the soil stratigraphy, groundwater conditions, and engineering properties of the ground. Minimum investigation requirements include: borings at intervals not exceeding 30 m (100 ft) along the wall alignment and extending at least 1.5 times the wall height below the proposed base; at least one boring at each end of the wall and at major changes in alignment or grade; SPT sampling at 0.75-1.5 m intervals; and groundwater monitoring. Additional investigation may include CPT soundings, geophysical surveys, and test pits. Critical items include identification of soft layers, groundwater conditions, obstructions (boulders, utilities), and corrosive ground conditions.
key_points: Borings at maximum 30 m (100 ft) intervals along wall alignment
Borings to minimum 1.5 times wall height below proposed base
At least one boring at each wall end and at major alignment changes

sections.title: Field Testing Procedures
sections.body: Field testing procedures include: (a) Standard Penetration Test (SPT) per ASTM D1586, the most common field test for soil nail wall investigations; (b) Cone Penetration Test (CPT) per ASTM D5778, useful for defining soil stratigraphy and estimating soil properties continuously with depth; (c) Vane Shear Test (VST) per ASTM D2573 for measuring undrained shear strength of soft to medium clays in situ; (d) Pressuremeter Test (PMT) per ASTM D4719; and (e) in-situ permeability tests. SPT N-values can be correlated to friction angle for granular soils and undrained shear strength for cohesive soils using established correlations.
key_points: SPT (ASTM D1586): most common field test for soil nail walls
CPT (ASTM D5778): continuous soil profiling and property estimation
Vane Shear (ASTM D2573): in-situ Su measurement for soft to medium clays
Pressuremeter Test (ASTM D4719) for deformation properties
In-situ permeability tests for groundwater assessment
SPT N-values correlated to friction angle and undrained shear strength

sections.title: Laboratory Testing
sections.body: Laboratory testing requirements include: (a) Classification tests: grain-size analysis (ASTM D422), Atterberg limits (ASTM D4318), moisture content (ASTM D2216), and unit weight (ASTM D7263); (b) Shear strength tests: direct shear (ASTM D3080), triaxial compression (ASTM D2850/D4767), and unconfined compression (ASTM D2166); (c) Corrosion-related tests: pH, resistivity, chloride content, sulfate content, and organic content. The selection of appropriate shear strength parameters (drained vs. undrained, peak vs. residual) depends on soil type, loading conditions, and expected strain levels.
key_points: Classification: grain-size (D422), Atterberg limits (D4318), moisture (D2216)
Shear strength: direct shear (D3080), triaxial (D2850/D4767), UC (D2166)
Corrosion tests: pH, resistivity, chloride, sulfate, organic content
Selection of drained vs undrained shear strength depends on soil type
Peak vs residual strength depends on expected strain levels

sections.title: Selection of Design Parameters
sections.body: Key design parameters include: (a) Unit weight: total and effective unit weights from lab measurements or correlations. (b) Shear strength: effective stress parameters (c', phi') for drained analysis of granular soils and long-term analysis of fine-grained soils; total stress parameters (Su) for short-term undrained analysis of fine-grained soils. (c) Bond strength (qu): the most critical parameter for soil nail design, representing the ultimate shear stress at the soil-grout interface. Preliminary bond strength values can be estimated from Tables 4.4a and 4.4b, which provide ranges based on soil type and drilling method. Final bond strengths must be verified by field pullout (verification and proof) tests during construction.

sections.title: Soil Creep Potential
sections.body: Soil creep can be a concern for permanent soil nail walls in fine-grained soils with high plasticity or high moisture content. Creep may cause long-term increase in nail tensile forces and wall deformation. Soils susceptible to creep include: clays with liquid limit greater than 50 (CH classification), clays with Liquidity Index (LI) greater than 0.2, and organic soils. When creep-susceptible soils are present, the design should account for potential long-term deformations using more conservative deformation estimates and more frequent monitoring.
key_points: Creep concern for permanent walls in high-plasticity fine-grained soils
May cause long-term increase in nail tensile forces

More frequent monitoring recommended

sections.title: Corrosion Potential Evaluation
sections.body: Evaluation of the ground corrosion potential is essential for permanent soil nail walls. Ground is considered aggressive (highly corrosive) if any of the following conditions exist: pH less than 4.5; resistivity less than 2,000 ohm-cm; chloride concentration greater than 200 ppm; sulfate concentration greater than 1,000 ppm; or presence of stray electrical currents. Testing standards are listed in Table 4.7. For aggressive ground, enhanced corrosion protection (encapsulation) is required per Chapter 7. For non-aggressive ground, simpler protection measures (epoxy coating or increased grout cover) may be adequate.
key_points: Ground aggressive if: pH < 4.5, resistivity < 2,000 ohm-cm
Aggressive if: chloride > 200 ppm, sulfate > 1,000 ppm
Aggressive if stray electrical currents present
Enhanced corrosion protection (encapsulation) for aggressive ground
Simpler protection (epoxy coating, grout cover) for non-aggressive ground

sections.title: Frost Potential
sections.body: Frost penetration can affect soil nail walls by: (a) generating frost heave pressures on the facing; (b) reducing bond strength in the frost zone; and (c) causing ice lenses that reduce soil strength upon thawing. The frost depth must be determined for each project location. Soil nails should be designed such that effective bond length begins below the frost depth. The facing design should account for potential frost pressures, and adequate drainage is critical to minimize water availability for ice lens formation.
key_points: Frost heave pressures can act on facing
Bond strength reduced in frost zone
Ice lenses reduce soil strength upon thawing
Effective bond length should begin below frost depth
Facing design must account for frost pressures
Adequate drainage minimizes ice lens formation

sections.title: Seismic Data
sections.body: Seismic design parameters must be obtained for all soil nail wall projects in seismically active regions. Required parameters include: site classification based on average shear wave velocity in the upper 30 m (Eq. 4.1) or average SPT N-value (Eq. 4.2) per AASHTO (2014) and MCEER/ATC-49; Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) from AASHTO seismic hazard maps; site-adjusted PGA using site coefficients FPGA (Table 4.9) and Fv (Table 4.10); and the design seismic coefficient kh for pseudo-static analysis. The design PGA is calculated as PGA_D = FPGA * PGA (Eq. 4.3), and the design spectral acceleration parameter S_D1 = Fv * S1 (Eq. 4.4).
